judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause purports to list every way employment ends but runs 'the first to occur of any of the events set forth in Sections 6.4 through 6.5', omitting termination for Cause (6.2) and for death or Disability (6.3) — an enumeration error visible on the face of the provision.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Limb (ii), automatic termination 'upon the consummation of a Liquidity Event', cannot be reconciled with Section 2.4(a) (bonus payable only if 'employed by the Company at the time of consummation') or with 2.4(d) (deferred payment conditioned on 'remaining as an employee'), and its omission of 6.2 and 6.3 conflicts with those sections' express termination rights.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Cause' is defined by a run-on list containing genuinely elastic terms — 'conduct causing the Company or its subsidiaries substantial public disgrace or disrepute', 'misappropriation (which shall not include incidental personal use of supplies)' — and the fifteen-day 'opportunity to cure such failure' is ambiguous as to whether it attaches to every listed ground or only to the failure-to-perform ground.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It measures duties by 'Schedule 2.1 hereof', a schedule not part of the instrument, promises 'Base Salary and Bonus' when no 'Bonus' is defined anywhere, refers to 'state or federal laws' in an agreement whose tax clause (7.6) invokes only Indian law, and 6.1 does not list 6.2 as a termination trigger.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Disability' is given a numeric test (120 days in any 240) but qualified by 'substantially failed to perform his essential duties ... with or without reasonable accommodation', and the surviving text is fragmentary as to what Base Salary continues after a Disability termination.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It promises Base Salary 'but not any Bonus' for the remainder of the year although 'Bonus' is nowhere defined, and Section 6.1 omits 6.3 from its list of events on which employment terminates.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Good Reason' is defined by a list whose limbs are damaged and open-ended — 'a material diminution ... in the Employee's position, duties, authority, or responsibilities, as outlined in Section 2.1' and 'a breach by the Company of the compensation and benefit provisions' — with 'material' and 'diminution' both undefined.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The severance measure is 'the Base Salary and Bonus' for the remainder of the Term, but no 'Bonus' is defined in Section 2.2 or elsewhere; the diminution test points to Section 2.1, whose content lives in the missing Schedule 2.1, and 2.4(b) layers a separate 1.75% payment on the same trigger.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The notice mechanics are reasonably definite (effective on a date chosen by the Company, no later than thirty business days after receipt), but the closing sentence says benefits continue only if 'allowed by' state or federal law where the parallel clauses say 'required by'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: That 'allowed'/'required' divergence from 6.2 and 6.4 is a real inconsistency, and like those clauses it invokes 'state or federal laws' and an undefined 'Bonus' in a contract performed in India and taxed under Indian law per 7.6.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A boilerplate headings clause with a single, definite effect; no term in it carries competing meanings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It simply neutralises the section headings elsewhere (including the 'Liquidity Event Bonus' heading in 2.4) and contradicts nothing.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only a fragment survives ('...deemed to be invalid or unenforceable ... provisions of this Agreement shall be unaffected'), but as a standard severability clause its operation is conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interacts with the many 'to the extent permitted by law' qualifiers (4.1, 7.4, 7.11) without contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The recoverable text is standard no-waiver language limiting any waiver to 'the specific instance and for the specific purpose for which the waiver was given'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with the writing requirement in 7.8 and the cure/notice mechanics in 6.2 without any tension I could find.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause bars assignment by the Employee but permits it by the Company 'only' in two enumerated corporate events, then closes with the usual heirs-and-personal-representatives sentence — an expressio unius list whose closed character could be argued over.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The permitted assignment events (merger, sale of substantially all assets, becoming a subsidiary) overlap the Liquidity Event definition in 2.4(c) but are framed around 'the Company' while 2.4 is framed around MiraMed, and the binding-on-heirs sentence sits against 7.11's ban on alienation of benefits.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Delivery methods and deemed-receipt language are ordinary; 'duly addressed to the appropriate party at the address indicated below' is definite because addresses are set out.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The address block for notices 'to the Company' gives Ajuba International, LLC/MiraMed Global Services in Jackson, Michigan, whereas the preamble makes the Company the Indian entity Ajuba Solutions (India) Pvt Ltd — a mismatch that bears directly on which entity is the counterparty.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One sentence, one rule: all payments are subject to withholding 'as required by Indian law'; nothing in it is capable of two readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It presupposes an Indian-law employment relationship while Sections 6.2, 6.4 and 6.5 condition benefit continuation on 'state or federal laws or regulations' (US concepts) and the Agreement has no governing-law clause at all, leaving a genuine whole-instrument mismatch.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause preserves 'the ongoing provisions of this Agreement, which shall survive such termination in accordance with their [terms]' without identifying which provisions are 'ongoing' — a self-referential vagueness that must be resolved by construction.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Which clauses survive matters concretely here: Articles 3 and 4 impose post-termination duties, 7.12 runs 'thereafter', and 2.4(b) pays after termination, so a court would have to supply the list the clause omits.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The integration language is standard, but the clause is drafted as superseding agreements 'entered into between the Company, Parent and the Employee' — bringing a non-signatory Parent within an agreement to which it is not a party — and its closing sentence is truncated mid-thought.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.4(a) states the Contingent Payout is 'in lieu of any amounts otherwise payable to you on account of any prior agreements entered into by you and the Company or MiraMed', which presupposes prior agreements with continuing effect that this clause purports to supersede, and the reference to Parent sits against 7.9's denial of third-party rights.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The surviving text is a bare statement that the Agreement is not intended to confer rights or remedies on anyone other than the parties; truncated, but its rule is single-valued.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Agreement nonetheless leans heavily on non-parties — Section 2.4 makes the whole bonus turn on MiraMed's transactions, 7.8 recites an integration involving Parent, 7.12 protects 'affiliates', and the signature page shows Tony Mira signing for Ajuba International, LLC — so who may enforce is a live question this clause answers only in one direction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Plain counterparts language with a single operative effect; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No other provision addresses execution formalities beyond 7.8's writing requirement, with which it is consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list 'sale, transfer, alienation, assignment, pledge, collateralization or attachment' is enumerated and specific, though 'benefits under this Agreement' is not defined and could be read to reach the Contingent Payout as well as plan benefits.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 7.4 makes the Agreement binding on and inuring to the parties' heirs and personal representatives, and 6.3 contemplates payments in respect of the Employee's death, which sit uneasily with a flat ban on any alienation or transfer of benefits.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause protects each party's officers, directors 'or employers' — plainly a mistyping of 'employees', which changes the class protected — and 'disparage' is left undefined while the obligation runs 'during the Employment Term and thereafter', i.e. perpetually.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reads with 3.3 (Company non-disclosure 'except for legitimate business purposes') and 7.7 (survival of 'ongoing provisions'), and its extension to 'affiliates' cuts against 7.9's no-third-party-beneficiary rule, but no provision squarely contradicts it.
